cse-1994-a-3-11.approach: Compare what each kind of independence must survive: a physical-schema change only has to be hidden by the internal/conceptual mapping, while a conceptual-schema change must be hidden from external views and application programs.

steps.title: Physical data independence
steps.body: Changing storage structures, files or indexes only alters the **conceptual–internal mapping**. Applications see the same conceptual schema, so this is routinely achieved by every DBMS.

steps.title: Logical data independence
steps.body: Changing the **conceptual schema** (adding/removing/splitting relations or attributes) must be hidden by the **external–conceptual mapping**. Application programs often reference the logical structure directly, so many such changes break them.

steps.title: Verdict
steps.body: Logical data independence is **harder** to achieve than physical data independence, so the statement is **False**.

answer.value: **False** — logical data independence is harder to achieve than physical data independence.

pitfalls: Swapping the two definitions: physical = storage-level changes, logical = conceptual-schema changes.
cse-1994-a-3-11.verification: Standard textbook statement (Elmasri–Navathe, Silberschatz): physical independence is easier and more common.

cse-1994-a-3-12.approach: Use $A^{-1}=\dfrac{\operatorname{adj}A}{\det A}$: compute the determinant, the cofactors, transpose, divide, and check $AA^{-1}=I$.

steps.title: Determinant
steps.body:
Expanding along row 1:
$$\det A = 1\,(1\cdot0-1\cdot1) - 0 + 1\,((-1)\cdot1-1\cdot0) = -1 + (-1) = -2.$$

steps.title: Adjoint and inverse
steps.body: $$\operatorname{adj}A = C^T = \begin{pmatrix}-1&1&-1\\0&0&-2\\-1&-1&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad A^{-1}=\frac{1}{-2}\operatorname{adj}A=\begin{pmatrix}1/2&-1/2&1/2\\0&0&1\\1/2&1/2&-1/2\end{pmatrix}.$$

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Row 1 of $A^{-1}$ times the columns of $A$: $\tfrac12+\tfrac12+0=1$, $0-\tfrac12+\tfrac12=0$, $\tfrac12-\tfrac12+0=0$. Rows 2 and 3 similarly give $(0,1,0)$ and $(0,0,1)$, so $A^{-1}A=I$.

pitfalls: Forgetting the checkerboard signs on cofactors.
Forgetting to transpose the cofactor matrix.
cse-1994-a-3-12.verification: Multiplied $A^{-1}A$ row by row and obtained the identity.

cse-1994-a-3-13.approach: The claim "$p\Leftrightarrow q$ does not imply $p\to\neg q$" is true iff some truth-table row makes $p\Leftrightarrow q$ true and $p\to\neg q$ false.

steps.title: Truth table
steps.body:
| $p$ | $q$ | $p\Leftrightarrow q$ | $p\to\neg q$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | T | **F** |
| T | F | F | T |
| F | T | F | T |
| F | F | T | T |

steps.title: Look for a counterexample row
steps.body: In row 1 ($p=q=T$) the premise $p\Leftrightarrow q$ is **T** but $p\to\neg q$ is **F**. So $p\Leftrightarrow q \Rightarrow p\to\neg q$ is not a tautology, i.e. the implication fails.

steps.title: Verdict
steps.body: Hence "$p\Leftrightarrow q$ does **not** imply $p\to\neg q$" is **True**.

answer.value: **True** — at $p=q=T$, $p\Leftrightarrow q$ is true but $p\to\neg q$ is false.

pitfalls: Answering about the implication itself ("false") rather than about the statement "does not imply" ("true").
cse-1994-a-3-13.verification: Only one row is needed as a counterexample; rechecked $p\to\neg q$ at $p=q=T$ is $T\to F = F$.

steps.title: Substitute
steps.body: $A*A = A\cdot A + \overline{A}\cdot\overline{A} = A + \overline{A}$ (idempotence).

steps.title: Simplify
steps.body: $A+\overline{A}=1$ (complement law), so $A*A=1$ — every value equals itself.

cse-1994-a-27-a-ii.approach: Since $*$ is XNOR and XNOR is associative with $A*A=1$ and $1*B=B$, $C*A=(A*B)*A=B$.

steps.title: Algebra
steps.body: XNOR is commutative and associative, so $C*A=(A*B)*A=(A*A)*B=1*B$. And $1*B = 1\cdot B+0\cdot\overline{B}=B$.

answer.value: $C * A = B$

pitfalls: Reading the second term as $\overline{AB}$ instead of $\overline{A}\,\overline{B}$ makes $*$ constantly 1.
cse-1994-a-27-a-ii.verification: Algebraic derivation and the 4-row truth table agree.

cse-1994-a-27-b.approach: Start from the equation that equals 0: a sum is 0 only when every term is 0, which pins B and forces the first equation.
concepts: OR is 0 iff all terms are 0

steps.title: Second equation
steps.body: $AC+B=0 \Rightarrow B=0$ and $AC=0$.

steps.title: First equation
steps.body: With $B=0$: $AB+\overline{A}C = 0+\overline{A}C = 1 \Rightarrow \overline{A}=1,\ C=1$, i.e. $A=0,\ C=1$.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: $AC = 0\cdot1=0$ ✓. $AB+\overline{A}C=0+1\cdot1=1$ ✓, $AC+B=0+0=0$ ✓. The solution is unique.

cse-1994-a-28.approach: Induct on the number of internal nodes $n$: replacing one leaf by an internal node with three leaf children adds one internal node and a net of two leaves.

steps.title: Claim
steps.body: Let $L(n)$ be the number of leaves of a 3-ary tree with $n\ge1$ internal nodes. Claim: $L(n)=2(n-1)+3=2n+1$.

steps.title: Base case
steps.body: $n=1$: the root with its three children; $L(1)=3=2(1-1)+3$ ✓.

steps.title: Inductive step
steps.body:
Let $T$ have $n+1\ge2$ internal nodes. Pick an internal node $v$ all of whose children are leaves (the deepest internal node). Deleting its three children makes $v$ a leaf: tree $T'$ has $n$ internal nodes and $L(T)-3+1=L(T)-2$ leaves. By hypothesis $L(T)-2=2(n-1)+3$, so
$$L(T)=2(n-1)+3+2=2n+3=2((n+1)-1)+3.$$

steps.title: Why the printed "2(n−1)" fails
steps.body: For $n=1$ it gives $0$ leaves, but the tree has 3 — so the intended statement is $2(n-1)+3$.

answer.value: Number of leaves $=2(n-1)+3=2n+1$ (proved by induction on $n$).

cse-1994-a-28.shortcut: Count edges: each internal node has 3 child edges, so $3n$ edges; a tree on $n+L$ nodes has $n+L-1$ edges. $3n=n+L-1 \Rightarrow L=2n+1$.
pitfalls: Using any internal node in the inductive step — it must be one whose three children are all leaves.
cse-1994-a-28.verification: Edge-count argument $3n=n+L-1$ gives the same $L=2n+1$; small cases $n=2\Rightarrow5$ leaves.

cse-1994-a-29.approach: Recognise exponentiation by squaring: $x^n = x^{n\bmod 2}\cdot (x^2)^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$, then prove it by strong induction on $n$.

steps.title: Base case
steps.body: $n=0$: the `if` is skipped, `what = 1 = x^0`.

steps.title: Inductive step
steps.body: For $n>0$ write $n = 2\lfloor n/2\rfloor + (n\bmod2)$. The function returns $x^{\,n\bmod 2}\cdot \text{what}(x^2,\lfloor n/2\rfloor)$, and by hypothesis $\text{what}(x^2,\lfloor n/2\rfloor)=(x^2)^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}=x^{2\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$. The product is $x^{n}$.

steps.title: Example
steps.body: what(3, 5): odd → $3\cdot$what(9, 2); even → what(81, 1); odd → $81\cdot$what(6561, 0) $=81$. Total $3\cdot81=243=3^5$ ✓.

answer.value: $\text{what}(x,n)=x^n$ (for $n\ge0$), computed with $O(\log n)$ multiplications.

pitfalls: Thinking it computes $x^{2n}$ or $n\cdot x$ because of the $x*x$ argument.

cse-1994-a-30.approach: Cycle-leader rotation: element at index $j$ must receive the one at $(j+K)\bmod n$. Follow each cycle from start $i$, saving $A[i]$ in temp, until reaching $(n+i-K)\bmod n$ (the slot that receives temp). There are $\gcd(n,K)$ cycles, started at $i=0,1,\dots$ while $i<\min$, where min tracks the smallest index already touched.

steps.title: What each move does
steps.body: Left rotation by $K$: new $A[j]$ = old $A[(j+K)\bmod n]$. So inside a cycle we do `A[j] := A[(j + K) mod n]` and advance `j := (j + K) mod n`.

steps.title: When a cycle ends
steps.body: The cycle started at $i$ closes when $j$ reaches the index whose source is $i$, i.e. $(j+K)\bmod n = i \iff j=(n+i-K)\bmod n$. So the inner loop runs `while j <> (n + i - K) mod n`, and afterwards `A[(n + i - K) mod n] := temp`.

steps.title: Moving to the next cycle
steps.body: The cycle from 0 visits exactly the multiples of $g=\gcd(n,K)$, so the smallest non-zero index it touches is $g$, recorded in min. Cycles start at $i=0,1,\dots,g-1$: outer loop `while i < min`, and `i := i + 1`. Every element is moved once, so time is $O(n)$ with $O(1)$ extra space.

steps.title: Example
steps.body: $n=6, K=2$: cycle from 0: $0\leftarrow2\leftarrow4$, then $A[4]:=$temp; min $=2$. Cycle from 1: $1\leftarrow3\leftarrow5$, $A[5]:=$temp. $i=2$ is not $<2$, stop. Result $[a_2,a_3,a_4,a_5,a_0,a_1]$ ✓.

answer.value: Blanks in order: `i < min`; `j <> (n + i - K) mod n`; `A[(j + K) mod n]`; `temp`; `i + 1`.

pitfalls: Using `i < n` for the outer loop — that re-rotates elements already placed.
Writing `A[(j - K) mod n]`, which rotates right.
cse-1994-a-30.verification: Hand-traced $n=6,K=2$ and $n=5,K=2$ (single cycle, min becomes 1 so only $i=0$ runs).

cse-1994-a-31.approach: Pre-order numbering means node 1 is the root and each subtree occupies a contiguous block of numbers; in post-order a subtree's root comes last in its block. Peel off subtrees from the post-order sequence.

steps.title: Root
steps.body: Pre-order starts with 1 and post-order ends with 1, so **1 is the root**. Remaining post-order: 3 5 4 2 | 7 8 6 | 10 11 12 9.

steps.title: First child: 2
steps.body: Pre-order next is 2; in post-order 2 appears after {3, 5, 4}, so the subtree of 2 is {2, 3, 4, 5}. Inside it, pre-order 3 then post-order shows 3 alone first ⇒ 3 is a leaf child of 2. Then 4 with post-order {5, 4} ⇒ 5 is a child of 4.

steps.title: Second child: 6
steps.body: Pre-order next is 6; post-order block {7, 8, 6} ⇒ 7 and 8 are leaf children of 6.

steps.title: Third child: 9
steps.body: Remaining block {10, 11, 12, 9} with root 9 (first in pre-order, last in post-order). Since 10, 11, 12 appear in the same order in both traversals, each is a leaf child of 9.

pitfalls: Assuming a binary tree — the root has three children here.
cse-1994-a-31.verification: Re-traversed the drawn tree: pre-order gives 1…12 and post-order gives 3 5 4 2 7 8 6 10 11 12 9 1.

cse-1994-b-32.approach: In the (7,4) Hamming code the check bits sit at positions 1, 2, 4; recompute the three even-parity checks — the failing checks, read as a binary number, give the position of the erroneous bit.

steps.title: Locate and correct
steps.body: Syndrome $c_4c_2c_1 = 110_2 = 6$ ≠ 0, so the message is **incorrect** and **bit 6** is wrong. Flip it 0 → 1: corrected word (bits 7…1) = **1100110**. Recheck after the flip: positions 1,3,5,7: $0+1+0+1=2$; 2,3,6,7: $1+1+1+1=4$; 4,5,6,7: $0+0+1+1=2$ — all even.

answer.value: The message is wrong: **bit 6** is in error; corrected message (bits 7…1) = **1100110**.

pitfalls: Reading the syndrome bits in the wrong order (011 = 3 would wrongly blame bit 3).
cse-1994-b-32.verification: All three parity checks are even after flipping bit 6.

cse-1994-b-33.approach: Add the low bytes with ADD, decimal-adjust with DAA, then add the high bytes with ADC so the decimal carry from the low byte propagates, and DAA again.

steps.title: Low two digits
steps.body:
```asm
MOV A, C   ; A = low byte of operand 1
ADD E      ; A = C + E (binary)
DAA        ; adjust to BCD, CY = decimal carry
MOV C, A   ; store low result
```

steps.title: High two digits
steps.body:
```asm
MOV A, B   ; A = high byte of operand 1
ADC D      ; A = B + D + CY
DAA        ; adjust to BCD
MOV B, A   ; store high result
HLT
```

steps.title: Why it works
steps.body: DAA after an addition adds 06h to a nibble that exceeds 9 (or produced an auxiliary carry) and 60h to the high nibble when needed, setting CY on a decimal carry. Example: $0958+0047$: low $58+47=9Fh$ → DAA → $05$, CY = 1; high $09+00+1=0Ah$ → DAA → $10$. Result BC = $1005$ ✓.

answer.value: `MOV A,C; ADD E; DAA; MOV C,A; MOV A,B; ADC D; DAA; MOV B,A; HLT` — result in BC.

pitfalls: Using ADD instead of ADC for the high byte, which drops the carry between digit pairs.
DAA works only on the accumulator after an addition.

cse-1994-b-34.approach: Read the excitation of each flip-flop from Fig. 5 ($J_2=\overline{Q_0}$, $K_2=1$, $D_1=Q_2$, $T_0=Q_1$) and step the state table four clocks, using the present-state values for every input.
cse-1994-b-34.given:
| FF | Input(s) | Next state |
|---|---|---|
| JK ($Q_2$) | $J=\overline{Q_0},\ K=1$ | $Q_2^+=J\overline{Q_2}=\overline{Q_0}\,\overline{Q_2}$ |
| D ($Q_1$) | $D=Q_2$ | $Q_1^+=Q_2$ |
| T ($Q_0$) | $T=Q_1$ | $Q_0^+=Q_0\oplus Q_1$ |

steps.title: Next-state equations
steps.body: With $K=1$ the JK flip-flop gives $Q_2^+ = J\overline{Q_2}+\overline{K}Q_2 = \overline{Q_0}\,\overline{Q_2}$. Also $Q_1^+=Q_2$ and $Q_0^+=Q_0\oplus Q_1$.

answer.value: After four clock pulses $Q_2Q_1Q_0 = 011$.

pitfalls: Using an already-updated value of $Q_2$ when computing $Q_1$ in the same clock — all flip-flops sample simultaneously.
cse-1994-b-34.verification: Recomputed each pulse directly from JK/D/T behaviour (J=K=1 toggles, J=0,K=1 resets) — same sequence 000→100→010→101→011.

cse-1994-b-35-a.approach: Classic XOR swap: three XORs alternating the destination, using $x\oplus x=0$ and $x\oplus0=x$.

steps.title: Sequence
steps.body:
Let initially $R_1=a,\ R_2=b$. Recall `XOR Ri, Rj` sets $R_j\leftarrow R_i\oplus R_j$.

1. `XOR R1, R2`: $R_2 = a\oplus b$
2. `XOR R2, R1`: $R_1 = (a\oplus b)\oplus a = b$
3. `XOR R1, R2`: $R_2 = b\oplus(a\oplus b) = a$

steps.title: Result
steps.body: Now $R_1=b$, $R_2=a$: the contents are exchanged without any extra register.

answer.value: `XOR R1, R2` ; `XOR R2, R1` ; `XOR R1, R2`

pitfalls: Mixing up source and destination: here the second operand $R_j$ is the destination.
cse-1994-b-35-a.verification: Checked with $a=1010_2, b=0110_2$: after the three steps $R_1=0110$, $R_2=1010$.

cse-1994-b-35-b.approach: A stuck-at-1 test must (1) drive $p$ to 0 in the good circuit (activate the fault) and (2) make the other input of the second NAND non-controlling (1) so the change at $p$ reaches the output.

steps.title: Activate
steps.body: $p=\overline{AB}=0$ in the good circuit requires $A=1,\ B=1$.

steps.title: Propagate
steps.body: The output is $\overline{p\,C}$. For $p$ to matter, $C$ must be 1 (a 0 on a NAND input forces the output to 1).

steps.title: Compare
steps.body: With $A=B=C=1$: good output $=\overline{0\cdot1}=1$; faulty ($p=1$) output $=\overline{1\cdot1}=0$. They differ, so the fault is detected.

answer.value: Test vector $A=1,\ B=1,\ C=1$ (good output 1, faulty output 0).

pitfalls: Setting $C=0$, which masks $p$.
cse-1994-b-35-b.verification: This is the only detecting vector: $p=0$ needs $A=B=1$ and propagation needs $C=1$.

cse-1994-b-36-a.approach: Set difference: all roll numbers minus those registered for course 322.

steps.title: Students registered for 322
steps.body: $R_{322}=\pi_{rollno}(\sigma_{cno=322}(\text{REGISTERED\_FOR}))$.

steps.title: Subtract from all students
steps.body: $\pi_{rollno}(\text{STUDENTS}) - R_{322}$ — both sides are union-compatible (single attribute rollno).

steps.title: Why not select cno ≠ 322
steps.body: $\sigma_{cno\neq322}$ would keep a student who registered for 322 **and** some other course, and would miss students registered for no course at all.

answer.value: $\pi_{rollno}(\text{STUDENTS}) - \pi_{rollno}(\sigma_{cno=322}(\text{REGISTERED\_FOR}))$

pitfalls: Using $\sigma_{cno\ne322}$ instead of set difference.
cse-1994-b-36-a.verification: Small instance: S1 in {322, 101}, S2 in {101}, S3 in none → result {S2, S3}, as required.

cse-1994-b-36-b.approach: Group STUDENTS by year and take MIN(age) in each group.

steps.title: Query
steps.body:
```sql
SELECT year, MIN(age)
FROM STUDENTS
GROUP BY year;
```

steps.title: Why it is correct
steps.body: GROUP BY year forms one group per year; MIN(age) is the youngest student's age in that group, so each output row is (year, age of youngest).

answer.value: `SELECT MIN(age), year FROM STUDENTS GROUP BY year;`

pitfalls: Selecting a non-grouped column such as sname without aggregation is invalid SQL.
cse-1994-b-36-b.verification: Only grouped or aggregated columns appear in the SELECT list.

cse-1994-b-37-a.approach: Read the occupancy from Fig. 7: leaves hold 2–4 keys, so $d=2$; the root already has $2d=4$ keys and the last leaf is full. An insertion into a full leaf splits it, the separator overflows the root, and the root splits, adding a level.

steps.title: Leaf split
steps.body: 100 (larger than all keys) goes to the last leaf, which already has $2d=4$ keys. With 5 keys it splits into leaves of 2 and 3 keys (or 3 and 2); the first key of the new right leaf is **copied** up as a separator.

steps.title: Root overflow
steps.body: The root receives a 5th key and a 6th child pointer, exceeding $2d=4$. It splits into two internal nodes of $d=2$ keys each, and the middle key is **moved** up.

steps.title: New root
steps.body: The moved key forms a new root with one key and two children, so the tree grows from 2 to 3 levels: new root → 2 internal nodes (3 children each) → 6 linked leaves.

answer.value: Last leaf splits (separator copied up), the full root then splits and its middle key becomes a **new root**: height grows from 2 to 3 levels (1 root key, 2 internal nodes of 2 keys, 6 leaves).

pitfalls: Copying vs moving: leaf splits copy the separator, internal splits move it.
cse-1994-b-37-a.verification: The exact key values cannot be read from the scan; the structural result follows from the occupancies alone.

cse-1994-b-37-b.approach: A search visits one node per level; every non-root node has at least $d+1$ children, so the height is logarithmic base $d$ in the number of leaves.

steps.title: Fan-out
steps.body: A node with between $d$ and $2d$ keys has between $d+1$ and $2d+1$ children.

steps.title: Height
steps.body: With $n$ leaves, level $h$ above the leaves has at most $n/(d+1)^h$ nodes, so the height is at most $\lceil\log_{d+1} n\rceil+1$.

steps.title: Search cost
steps.body: One node per level is accessed: $O(\log_{d} n)$ nodes.

answer.value: $O(\log_d n)$

cse-1994-b-37-b.verification: Bases $d$ and $d+1$ differ only by a constant factor for $d\ge2$.

cse-1994-b-37-c.approach: Proof without words: going from a $k\times k$ square to a $(k+1)\times(k+1)$ square adds an L-shaped border of $2k+1$ dots, so stacking borders $k=0,\dots,n-1$ builds an $n\times n$ square.

steps.title: One border
steps.body: An L-border around a $k\times k$ square has one row of $k+1$ dots plus a column of $k$ more: $(k+1)+k=2k+1$ dots, and $(k+1)^2-k^2=2k+1$.

steps.title: Stacking
steps.body: Start with 1 dot ($k=0$, $2\cdot0+1$). Adding borders $k=1,2,\dots,n-1$ gives squares of $4, 9, \dots, n^2$ dots.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: The $n\times n$ square is exactly the union of the borders, so $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}(2i+1)=n^2$. (Algebraically: $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}((i+1)^2-i^2)=n^2-0$ telescopes.)

answer.value: Each L-border adds $2k+1$ dots to a $k\times k$ square to give $(k+1)^2$; the borders for $k=0..n-1$ tile the $n\times n$ square, so $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}(2i+1)=n^2$.

cse-1994-b-37-d.approach: Split the odd-number sum into $2\sum i + n$, equate to $n^2$ from part (a), solve for $\sum i$, then add $n$.

answer.value: $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}(2i+1)=2\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} i + n = n^2 \Rightarrow \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} i = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}$; adding $n$ gives $\sum_{i=1}^{n} i=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$.

cse-1994-b-38.approach: A ring where every element is idempotent is a Boolean ring. Squaring $a+a$ shows $a=-a$; squaring $a+b$ then gives $ab=-ba=ba$.

steps.title: Characteristic 2
steps.body: $(a+a)^2=a+a$. Expanding: $a^2+a^2+a^2+a^2=4a$, so $4a=2a \Rightarrow 2a=0$, i.e. $a=-a$ for every $a$.

steps.title: Square a + b
steps.body: $(a+b)^2=a+b$. Expanding: $a^2+ab+ba+b^2=a+ab+ba+b$. Cancelling $a+b$: $ab+ba=0$.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.body: $ab=-ba=ba$ (using $x=-x$ for $x=ba$). Hence the ring is **commutative**.

answer.value: Yes — the ring is commutative ($ab+ba=0$ and $x=-x$ give $ab=ba$).

pitfalls: Assuming a multiplicative identity — the proof does not need one.
cse-1994-b-38.verification: Example: the power set ring with symmetric difference and intersection is idempotent and commutative.
